title: NVIDIA Q4 FY2025 Earnings Call Transcript

sections.prepared_remarks: NVIDIA reporting record quarter — revenue $39.3 billion, up 122 percent year over year. Data Center revenue $35.6 billion, up 409 percent. We are in the industrial revolution of AI. Every major cloud provider and enterprise is scaling AI infrastructure with NVIDIA. Blackwell architecture shipped 13,000 units in Q4 alone — the fastest product ramp in our company's history. Our supply chain has expanded substantially with new partners across CoWoS-L packaging, HBM3e memory, and copper interconnect. Data center revenue came from a diverse customer base — Hyperscalers: Microsoft Azure, Amazon AWS, Google Cloud, Meta — represent roughly half of Data Center. Enterprise and sovereign AI represent the other half — industries from automotive to healthcare to financial services deploying AI at scale. NVIDIA NIM microservices are now available — enterprises can deploy AI inference infrastructure that runs optimized inference containers for every major model family. Our inference pipeline revenue is significant and growing. We have $100 billion in forward backlog. We are launching Blackwell Ultra in H2 2025 with 1.5x the performance of B200.
sections.financial_highlights: Revenue $39.3 billion, EPS $0.89, gross margin 73.5 percent. Compute revenue $33.5 billion, Networking $5.4 billion with InfiniBand and Spectrum-X strong. We expect Q1 FY2026 revenue of $43 billion, plus or minus 2 percent. We expect gross margins in the mid-70s. Data Center for full fiscal year reached $115 billion. Gaming revenue $2.5 billion, up 27 percent. Automotive $570 million, up 103 percent on autonomous driving and robotics contracts. We continued investing in R&D at $2.5 billion this quarter. We are launching new products every 12 months — Blackwell, Rubin in 2026, Rubin Ultra in 2027. The three-stage software moat — CUDA, NIM, and NEMO microservices — locks in enterprise customers for years. Our gross margins benefited from Blackwell ASP economics which exceed Hopper, though supply constraints will moderate in Q2.
sections.qanda_session:
Moses Mann: Jensen, when you talk about $100 billion backlog, can you characterize what's in it? And when does the backlog represent actual shipment schedule versus just customer intention? Do you have contractual commitments from hyperscalers that lock in GPU allocation?

Jensen Huang: Moses, good question. Our backlog is primarily contractual commitments from hyperscalers and enterprise customers with binding purchase orders. The allocation process for GPUs is competitive — customers want allocation guarantees. We are prioritizing based on long-term partnerships, supply commitments, and enterprise commitments. What makes the backlog durable is our software ecosystem — once you're on CUDA, it takes years to move. Our Blackwell customers are writing software for the Hopper and Blackwell compute architecture, and they are planning multi-year deployments. So the backlog reflects genuine demand, not speculative ordering. That said, we keep our supply-demand visibility through quarterly dialogue with customers. The $100 billion is real — we've got binding orders from 30,000 to 40,000 customers globally.

Timothy Arcuri: Colette, on the gross margin — in the near term, you're seeing supply constraint benefit margins. As Blackwell production ramps to meet demand, how do margins trend over the next 4 to 6 quarters? And do we see a mix headwind from Blackwell Ultra versus standard Blackwell?

Colette Kress: Timothy, gross margins benefited from initial Blackwell production and supply-demand dynamics. As Blackwell production ramps through H1 2026, we expect gross margins to be in the 73 to 75 percent range. There will be a slight mix headwind as more Blackwell configurations become available, including Ultra in H2. But the overall margin profile is supported by data center scale and the NIM software attachment rate — software and services are higher margin. We expect our full-year gross margins to be durable in the mid-70s as we absorb the mix headwinds and production ramp. The key driver is that total Data Center revenue continues to grow rapidly, so the margin dollars expand even as percentage margins compress slightly.
sections.forward_outlook: Jensen Huang: The world is being re-platformed. Every company will need to run AI factories — massive GPU clusters that process data and produce intelligence. NVIDIA is the essential compute platform for this transformation. We've proven we can ship at volume with Blackwell. We have the supply chain, the software, and the roadmap. We are investing in three new categories: robotics, Omniverse for industrial digital twins, and autonomous vehicles. Each of these markets will be larger than our Data Center business within the decade. Our competitive position strengthens with each product generation because CUDA and the software ecosystem are compounding. We expect fiscal 2026 to be another exceptional year. The age of general robotics is beginning — humanoid robots trained in simulation will transform manufacturing.
